analysis.one_liner: Taxes the net wealth of people worth over $1 billion and spends it on health care, housing, child care, and teacher pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 2, 2026, with one Democratic cosponsor, and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would impose a 5% annual tax on the net worth of anyone holding more than $1 billion in assets, with mandatory IRS audits of at least half of covered taxpayers each year and a 60% exit tax on billionaires who renounce citizenship. The money would fund repealing the 2025 health law's coverage cuts and extending ACA premium subsidies, adding dental, hearing, and vision coverage to Medicare, $85.6 billion a year for affordable housing, a federal child care entitlement for low- and middle-income children under six, a $60,000 minimum salary for public school teachers, and investments in home-based long-term care. It has one cosponsor, sits in the Senate Finance Committee, and has had no action beyond referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families: seniors gain Medicare dental, hearing, and vision coverage; children in families earning up to 250% of state median income gain a federal child care entitlement; ACA enrollees gain broader and richer premium subsidies; renters gain an $85.6 billion-a-year affordable housing fund; public school teachers gain a $60,000 salary floor. Billionaires pay, via a 5% annual tax on net worth above $1 billion.

how_it_helps.text: Extends Medicare, for the first time, to cover dental care (cleanings, fillings, crowns, root canals, dentures, implants), hearing care including hearing aids, and routine vision exams and eyeglasses, starting in 2027-2028.
Repeals the health provisions of Public Law 119-21 (the 2025 reconciliation law) and removes the income cap on ACA premium tax credits while lowering premium contributions for every income tier.
Authorizes $85.6 billion per year for fiscal 2026-2035 for the Housing Trust Fund, which builds and preserves affordable rental housing for extremely low-income households.

Creates a federal entitlement to child care and early learning for every child under 6 in families earning up to 250% of their state's median income, with payment rates designed to cover the full cost of quality care and providers' payrolls.

Guarantees a $60,000-a-year minimum salary and collective bargaining rights for public school teachers, and funds home- and community-based care investments plus permanent spousal impoverishment protections for Medicaid home-care recipients.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and trusts with a net worth above $1 billion, who would pay 5% of their net value each year; billionaires who renounce citizenship would face a 60% tax on their assets. Wealthy nonresidents would pay on U.S. assets.

drawbacks.text: The 5% annual tax applies to the full net value of a billionaire's assets, not just to gains realized in a year, so owners of large illiquid holdings — like private company stakes — could face a bill larger than their annual cash income and might have to sell assets to pay it.

Valuing hard-to-price assets (private businesses, art, real estate) is inherently uncertain; the bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad discretion to set valuation rules, and disputes over those rules would likely produce years of litigation.

A federal tax on the value of property raises constitutional questions about whether Congress has power to tax unrealized gains without apportioning the tax among the states — questions the Supreme Court has recently entertained — so the tax could be struck down or narrowed even if enacted.

The spending side is enormous — $85.6 billion a year for housing plus open-ended child care and health entitlements — and it all rides on a narrow tax base of roughly several hundred households, so revenue projections would need to survive both avoidance and legal challenge to fund the programs permanently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: Medicare dental, hearing, and vision coverage, $85.6B a year for affordable housing, a near-universal child care entitlement, and a $60,000 teacher minimum. The costs fall on roughly 700 of the wealthiest U.S. households, who currently enjoy the tax system's biggest structural gap — unrealized gains that are never taxed. The strongest good-faith objections are real: taxing unrealized gains on illiquid assets (like stakes in private companies) could force owners to sell to pay the bill, asset valuation is inherently contentious, constitutional challenges are likely, and wealthy taxpayers would have powerful incentives and means to restructure holdings. But the bill's audit mandate, expatriation penalty, and valuation rules show the drafting anticipates those problems, and the spending side is the largest direct investment in ordinary families' health, housing, and child care on the table this Congress. The main honest criticism of the bill as a proposal is its scale and fragility: the required tax and spending are enormous by current standards, and the bill had no mechanism or support to reach a floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 2, 2026, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been taken since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 2, 2026 and read twice.
That same day it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no recorded action on it since.
It has a single cosponsor, one Senate Democrat, out of 45; no other senator from either party has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Billionaires whose wealth would have faced the 5% annual tax, since the bill shows no signs of advancing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Billionaires who would have owed the tax

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor in either chamber.

sides.party_line_note: With one cosponsor and no votes or committee action, no partisan breakdown exists; the bill's sponsor is an independent caucusing with Democrats, and no Republican or additional Democratic support is on the record.

industries.note: Roughly the several hundred taxpayers with net worth above $1 billion would owe 5% of their net worth annually — a transfer of tens of billions per year from concentrated wealth to public programs.

industries.industry: Closely held businesses owned by billionaires
industries.note: Privately held businesses 5%-owned by a billionaire would face new asset valuation and information reporting requirements, with penalties for noncompliance.

Medicare dental coverage would bring millions of new patients and a government fee schedule set at 70% of median private fees — new patient volume at lower per-service rates than most dentists charge privately.

industries.industry: Health insurers and ACA marketplace plans
industries.note: Repealing the reconciliation health provisions and lifting the premium credit income cap keeps millions of subsidized customers flowing through private marketplace plans rather than a public alternative.

The child care entitlement would create enormous demand for providers while requiring states to pay rates sufficient to cover full costs and quality standards — higher revenue with stricter operating requirements.

New Medicare coverage of hearing aids and eyeglasses brings beneficiaries as paying customers, but the bill subjects those devices to competitive bidding and payment caps tied to federal supply schedule rates, squeezing supplier margins.

industries.industry: Public school teachers and their unions
industries.note: The bill guarantees teachers a $60,000 minimum salary and collective bargaining rights — a direct wage gain for the profession, funded federally.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced by a single independent senator's office with one cosponsor, referred to Finance with no hearing or markup scheduled, almost never advance; the realistic path is that it sits in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote. Wealth tax proposals of this scale face steep hurdles even from moderate Democrats, and the Finance Committee's agenda is controlled by its chair, who has shown no indication of taking it up.
